title: Cognitive Integration: How Culture Transforms Us and Extends Our Cognitive Capabilities
central_proposition: The Cognitive Integration (CI) framework explains how human cognition is transformed and extended by cultural evolution and niche construction, through the acquisition of normative cognitive practices that reuse and reorient phylogenetically older sensorimotor capacities for manipulating symbolic representations.

concept_definitions.name: Cognitive Integration (CI)
concept_definitions.definition: A framework for understanding and studying cognition and the mind that draws on empirical research in embodied cognition, arguments for extended cognition, distributed cognition, niche construction and cultural inheritance, developmental psychology, social learning, and cognitive neuroscience, accounting for cognitive phenomena diachronically across both ontogenetic and phylogenetic time scales as well as synchronically on faster time scales.

concept_definitions.name: Cognitive Practices (CPs)
concept_definitions.definition: Cultural practices that are cognitive in nature, acquired through learning and training, transforming genetically endowed biological capacities and allowing individuals to think in ways that un-enculturated brains and bodies do not; they are normative patterned practices that regulate and govern brain-body-environment interactions.

concept_definitions.name: Dual Component Transformation
concept_definitions.definition: A process where learning histories transform both online and offline cognitive capacities, specifically involving the reorientation/redeployment of existing pattern recognition capacities to recognize symbols and existing sensorimotor abilities for manipulation and tool use to create and order symbols.

concept_definitions.name: Integrated Cognitive System (ICS)
concept_definitions.definition: A multilayered system with heterogeneous components, dynamically interwoven into a cooperative of processes and states, where coordination dynamics are understood in terms of physical brain-body-niche interactions and cognitive practices that govern these interactions.

concept_definitions.name: Normative Manipulations/Embodied Engagements
concept_definitions.definition: Specific bodily interactions with the environment that are not simply causal but are embodied practices developed through learning and training, governed by cognitive practices.

concept_definitions.name: Cognitive Transformation
concept_definitions.definition: The acquisition of a novel cognitive ability or the transformation of an existing capacity, resulting from the acquisition and embodiment of cognitive practices.

argument_structure: The paper first sketches the core commitments of CI, outlining its main criteria and dimensions. It then provides motivations for CI from both ontogenetic (representational complexity, dual component transformations) and phylogenetic (evolutionary continuity, niche construction, neural plasticity) perspectives. Finally, it differentiates CI from other 4E approaches and addresses recent criticisms regarding artifact extension, persistence of cognitive systems, and representationalism.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: CI proposes that phylogenetically older sensorimotor capacities, adapted for environmental interaction and tool use, are reused and reoriented through neural plasticity and social learning. This process, driven by cultural evolution and niche construction, leads to the acquisition of normative cognitive practices. These practices govern the manipulation of external symbolic representations, transforming existing cognitive abilities and enabling novel ones, thereby extending cognitive capabilities beyond the 'naked brain'. The resulting integrated cognitive system involves dynamic, interwoven brain-body-environment interactions regulated by these cultural norms.

findings.antecedent: Phylogenetically early sensorimotor interactions with the environment
findings.mechanism: These early forms of cognition are built upon by more recent cultural innovations, transforming and extending cognitive capabilities.
findings.quote: phylogenetically early forms of cognition, in humans, involve sensorimotor interactions with the environment; these are built upon by more recent cultural innovations
findings.empirical_support_cited: Trestman (2013) on Cambrian explosion, Pinel et al. (2004) on finger gnosis

findings.antecedent: Cultural innovations (symbolic representations, normative cognitive practices)
findings.mechanism: These innovations, products of cultural evolution and niche construction, are preserved across generations by cultural inheritance, transforming and extending human cognition.
findings.quote: The key cultural innovations are symbolic representations and the normative cognitive practices that govern their manipulation.

findings.antecedent: Phylogenetically early sensorimotor capacities (e.g., tool use)
findings.consequent: Ability to create and manipulate representations for cognitive tasks
findings.mechanism: These capacities are reused and reoriented through neural plasticity and social learning, leading to the transformation of cognitive capacities.
findings.quote: Phylogenetically early sensorimotor capacities for making and manipulating tools can be reused to create and manipulate representations when completing cognitive tasks.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Pinel et al. (2004), Venkatraman et al. (2005), Anderson and Penner-Wilger (2012)

findings.antecedent: Learning histories
findings.mechanism: Learning transforms both types of capacities, allowing for their integrated function in cognitive tasks.
findings.source: What is Cognitive Integration? An Initial Sketch
findings.quote: our learning histories transform both our online and offline capacities.

findings.antecedent: Growing complexity in social and physical environment
findings.mechanism: Environmental complexity, social complexity, social learning, hostility, and competition drive the expansion of cognitive capacities.
findings.source: What is Cognitive Integration? An Initial Sketch
findings.quote: Growing complexity in the social and physical environment drives the evolution of cognitive complexity

findings.antecedent: Cultural inheritance, high-fidelity social learning, cultural/social intelligence, neural plasticity, and redundancy
findings.consequent: Human uniqueness (e.g., creating complex social systems and representational systems)
findings.mechanism: The coevolution of these factors produces the 'human syndrome' for complex social and representational systems.
findings.source: What is Cognitive Integration? An Initial Sketch
findings.quote: The coevolution of these factors produces the human syndrome² for creating vast and complex social systems and systems of representation

findings.antecedent: Creation and deployment of representational systems and cognitive practices
findings.mechanism: Cognitive systems evolve through the active creation, maintenance, and manipulation of these external systems and practices.
findings.source: What is Cognitive Integration? An Initial Sketch
findings.quote: cognitive systems evolve through the creation and deployment of representational systems and the (cognitive) practices for 'creating, maintaining and manipulating' those systems

findings.antecedent: Social learning
findings.consequent: Spread of representational systems and cognitive practices
findings.mechanism: Modern humans have evolved high-fidelity learning capacities over long developmental periods, making social learning the primary mechanism for cultural transmission.
findings.source: What is Cognitive Integration? An Initial Sketch
findings.quote: The main mechanism for the spread of representational systems and cognitive practices is social learning.

findings.antecedent: Acquisition of cognitive practices (through learning and training)
findings.consequent: Transformation of genetically endowed biological capacities
findings.mechanism: CPs allow individuals to think and act in ways that un-enculturated brains and bodies cannot, by shaping the human mind and body through embodiment and internalization.
findings.quote: The practices are acquired through learning and training, transforming our genetically endowed biological capacities and allowing us to think in ways that our un-enculturated brains and bodies do not.

findings.antecedent: Normative patterned practices
findings.mechanism: CPs govern and determine the physical dynamics of brain-body-niche interactions over time, making them more specific and targeted at cognitive tasks.
findings.quote: coordination dynamics of the system are... understood in terms of CPs that govern and determine those interactions (over time).

findings.antecedent: Regular, patterned activities (cognitive practices)
findings.mechanism: Practices shape the mind and body through embodiment and internalization, and conversely, enacting practices shape and reshape norms, processes, institutions, and sociality.
findings.quote: A patterned practice approach assumes that regular, patterned activities shape the human mind and body through embodiment, and internalization.

findings.antecedent: Learning and training
findings.mechanism: Individuals embody cognitive practices by transforming or extending existing body schemas and motor programs, enabling new cognitive actions.
findings.quote: Individuals embody CPs? They do so by transforming body schemas or motor programs

findings.antecedent: Organism-environment relations (Biological Interactions)
findings.mechanism: Sensorimotor contingencies and animate perception are dependent on and altered by the environmental context and organism state; developing these requires training, expertise, and norms.
findings.quote: Organism-environment relations... sensorimotor contingencies and animate perception dependent on and altered by context of the environment and state of the organism

findings.antecedent: Language/exogenous props (Corrective Practices)
findings.mechanism: These props structure and channel behavior, aiding in self-correction and problem-solving.
findings.quote: Use of language/exogenous props to direct/structure practical actions toward achieving tasks (channeling behavior)

findings.antecedent: Using the environment as its own representation (Epistemic Practices)
findings.mechanism: These practices offload cognitive load by reducing memory load, time complexity, and error through movements in physical and abstract problem spaces.
findings.quote: Using the environment as its own representation. Movements not just in physical space but in an abstract problem space

findings.antecedent: Manipulations of external representations (Epistemic Tools and Representational Systems)
findings.mechanism: These manipulations are performed according to learned cognitive norms (purposive, corrective, manipulative, interpretative, creative), aiding in complex cognitive tasks.
findings.quote: Manipulations of external representations according to learned cognitive norms

findings.antecedent: Complex cognitive tasks (Blended Interactions)
findings.mechanism: These tasks involve combinations of multiple cognitive practices in cycles of cognitive processing.
findings.quote: Blended interactions are complex cognitive tasks that may involve combinations of practices in cycles of cognitive processing.

findings.antecedent: External representational systems for abstract and theoretical thinking
findings.mechanism: These systems, when manipulated using redeployed sensorimotor resources, enable humans to perform difficult and demanding cognitive tasks they otherwise could not.
findings.quote: The payoff from CI is twofold: the ability to do things that we otherwise cannot do and the transformation of existing abilities, making us smarter and better at difficult and demanding cognitive tasks.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Menary (2015a), De Cruz and De Smedt (2013)

findings.antecedent: Learning to create and manipulate symbols in physical space (e.g., writing, abacus use)
findings.mechanism: This learning process results in a dual transformation: the ability to recognize symbols and the ability to physically create and order them, rather than simple internalization.
findings.source: Ontogeny: Representational Complexity and Dual Component Transformations
findings.quote: This learning process results in a dual transformation of not just our ability to recognize symbols... but also our ability to create and physically order symbols on a physical medium

findings.antecedent: Regular spacing and ordering of symbols in algebraic equations (e.g., FOIL)
findings.mechanism: Mathematicians rely on the external structure and manipulation of symbols as part of their cognitive process, demonstrating that writing is partly constitutive of symbolic thought.
findings.source: Ontogeny: Representational Complexity and Dual Component Transformations
findings.quote: mathematicians rely upon the regular spacing and the FOIL (first, outer, inner, last) ordering of symbols in algebraic equations to be able to complete mathematical operations
findings.empirical_support_cited: Landy and Goldstone (2007), Landy et al. (2014), De Cruz and De Smedt (2013), Menary and Kirchhoff (2014)

findings.antecedent: Convergent evolution of phenotypic plasticity, neural plasticity, cultural inheritance, and language
findings.consequent: Human capacity to create and manipulate public symbol systems
findings.mechanism: These factors allowed existing cognitive systems to be reoriented through learning and training to perform new functions required for symbolic thought, without requiring new specialized systems.
findings.source: Phylogeny: The Evolutionary Case for ICs and the Evolutionary Continuity Condition
findings.quote: The answer lies in the convergent evolution of phenotypic plasticity, neural plasticity, cultural inheritance, and language that sprung from the need to adapt to variable environments and growing social complexity.

findings.antecedent: Organism-environment reciprocal coupling
findings.mechanism: Organisms are predisposed to manipulate and create their environmental niches, which is an adaptation.
findings.source: Phylogeny: The Evolutionary Case for ICs and the Evolutionary Continuity Condition
findings.quote: Organisms are reciprocally coupled to their environmental niches, resulting in an organism-environment system

findings.antecedent: Organism's manipulations of its environment (as adaptations)
findings.consequent: Basic kind of normativity and intentional directedness
findings.mechanism: These adaptive manipulations allow for sensitivity to salient environmental variables and lay the groundwork for more complex cognitive practices.
findings.source: Phylogeny: The Evolutionary Case for ICs and the Evolutionary Continuity Condition
findings.quote: That these manipulations are adaptations gives them a basic kind of normativity. This normativity allows for the beginnings of an organism's sensitivity to salient environmental variables.

findings.antecedent: Cultural systems (representation, manipulation methods)
findings.consequent: Fluent bodily manipulations of public representations
findings.mechanism: The role of culture, learned and practiced in ontogeny, allows humans to develop the repertoire for manipulating public representations, building on phylogenetic predispositions.
findings.source: Phylogeny: The Evolutionary Case for ICs and the Evolutionary Continuity Condition
findings.quote: The role of culture in providing systems of representation and methods for their manipulation must be learned and practiced before fluent bodily manipulations of public representations become part of a human's cognitive repertoire.

findings.antecedent: Cognitive practices acquired through learning
findings.mechanism: Artifacts become cognitively significant only when they can be manipulated via learned cognitive practices, rather than simply optimizing precision estimations.
findings.source: CI's Relations to other Approaches and Defending CI Against Objections
findings.quote: artifacts only become important insofar as we can manipulate them via cognitive practices acquired through learning.

findings.antecedent: Normative patterned practices and their embodiment
findings.mechanism: Unlike fleeting causal couplings, these practices are stable and persisting, structuring ICSs and making them enduring capacities of the organism.
findings.source: Rupert's Criticism of Persistent Cognitive Systems
findings.quote: the patterned practices and our embodiment of them are not fleeting, but stable and persisting.

findings.antecedent: Organism and environment
findings.mechanism: Phenotypes are 'constructed' in inherited developmental niches through the coevolution of organism and environment, rather than a one-way creation by the organism.
findings.source: Rupert's Criticism of Persistent Cognitive Systems
findings.quote: organism and environment coevolve over time, with phenotypes being 'constructed' in inherited developmental niches

findings.antecedent: Sensorimotor manipulations of mathematical notations
findings.mechanism: These manipulations are governed by public mathematical practices and are partly constitutive of understanding, rather than requiring internal representations of external content.
findings.quote: The sensorimotor manipulations of mathematical notations, for example, are partly constitutive of our understanding of mathematical practice.

findings.antecedent: Acquisition of online capacities to manipulate external symbols
findings.mechanism: Without this transformation, the ability to perform operations previously requiring external symbols in their absence would be a mystery.
findings.quote: If our capacities for offline symbolic thinking are not transformed by our acquisition of the online capacities to manipulate them, then it becomes a mystery as to how we are able to do so.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Neuroimaging studies could investigate the neural reuse of sensorimotor circuitry during symbolic manipulation tasks, comparing novices and experts to observe the transformation of capacities.

Developmental studies could track the acquisition of cognitive practices in children, observing how early exploratory interactions become scaffolded and how body schemas/motor programs are transformed.

Cross-cultural studies could compare cognitive performance on complex tasks (e.g., mathematics) in populations with different representational systems and cognitive practices, to demonstrate the transformative effect of cultural innovations.

Experiments could manipulate the availability and structure of external representational systems (e.g., different numeral systems, spatial arrangements of symbols) to measure their impact on cognitive load, error rates, and task completion time, providing evidence for cognitive offloading and the constitutive role of external manipulations.
bridge_warrants: CI integrates insights from embodied, embedded, extended, and enactive cognition by emphasizing sensorimotor interactions and the constitutive role of the environment.
CI connects with the extended synthesis in evolutionary biology by highlighting cultural evolution, niche construction, and cultural inheritance as drivers of cognitive change.
CI aligns with developmental systems theory by positing that cognitive capacities are 'constructed' in inherited developmental niches through organism-environment coevolution.

CI acknowledges predictive processing as a useful way to understand proximal brain mechanisms but rejects the free energy principle as an ultimate explanation for the enculturation of cognition, instead grounding it in cultural evolution and social learning.
methodological_critiques: The paper implicitly critiques definitions of cognition based on 'underived/original content' as too narrow or restrictive, and definitions based on 'information processing' as too broad, advocating for a dimensional analysis instead.

It critiques the 'artifact extension' model of the extended mind for not adequately accounting for cultural inheritance and the transformative role of cognitive practices, focusing too much on individually entrenched resources.
model_structure: The CI framework proposes a multilayered integrated cognitive system where phylogenetically older sensorimotor capacities are reused and reoriented by cultural innovations (symbolic representations, normative cognitive practices). This process, driven by social learning and neural plasticity, leads to a dual component transformation of both online and offline cognition. The system's coordination dynamics are governed by cognitive practices that regulate brain-body-niche interactions, resulting in the acquisition of novel cognitive abilities and the transformation of existing ones.
limitations: The paper acknowledges that the dimensional analysis of integration may not satisfy those seeking a simple set of necessary and sufficient criteria for cognition.

It notes that while CI is compatible with predictive processing at a neural level, it rejects the free energy principle as an ultimate explanation for the enculturation of cognition, which might be seen as a limitation by proponents of the free energy principle.

paper_metadata.title: Cognitive Integration
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Abstract
               If cognition is fundamentally interactive how did it come to be so? The cognitive integration framework provides an answer: phylogenetically early forms of cognition, in humans, involve sensorimotor interactions with the environment; these are built upon by more recent cultural innovations, which are a product of cultural evolution and niche construction. The key cultural innovations are symbolic representations and the normative cognitive practices that govern their manipulation. These representational systems and cognitive practices are preserved across generations by cultural inheritance. Phylogenetically early sensorimotor capacities for making and manipulating tools can be reused to create and manipulate representations when completing cognitive tasks. Reuse depends upon neural plasticity and social learning, which results in the transformation of our cognitive capacities. The chapter also provides a dimensional analysis of integrated cognitive systems and provides responses to recent criticisms.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper extends the Extended Mind Hypothesis by arguing that cultural practices and artifacts do not merely causally aid cognition but constitutively transform and integrate with cognitive processes, leading to novel cognitive capabilities, rather than just extending pre-existing ones.

The paper operates within the broader framework of 4E cognition, particularly emphasizing the extended and enactive aspects, to argue for a deeply integrated view of mind and world, mediated by culture.

The paper draws upon principles from cultural-historical psychology regarding the role of cultural tools and social interaction in shaping higher cognitive functions, reinterpreting them through the lens of cognitive integration.

mechanism_chain.description: Human cognition is fundamentally transformed and extended through active engagement with and integration of cultural practices, tools, and social environments. This process moves beyond mere scaffolding to a constitutive integration where cultural elements become part of the cognitive system itself, leading to novel cognitive capabilities.

steps.from_construct: Innate sensorimotor capacities and basic biological cognitive abilities
steps.to_construct: Engagement with cultural practices and artifacts (e.g., language, tools, social norms)

steps.from_construct: Engagement with cultural practices and artifacts
steps.to_construct: Integration and internalization of cultural elements into cognitive processes

steps.from_construct: Integration of cultural elements into cognitive processes
steps.to_construct: Emergence of extended and transformed human cognitive capabilities (e.g., abstract thought, complex memory, problem-solving)
